course: Traffic and Flow Diagram Automation with Claude
source_input: Client use case 9, "Traffic and Flow Diagram Automation": "Creation for traffic and flow diagram with the help of traceroute and ping access." The client's stated aim for all use cases: "Our Aim is to do automation using Claude for all these content", with course titles of the form "Automation of <> using Claude". Related use cases name the device estate: F5, NetScaler, Radware and Anaya LB load balancers, Cisco ACI, and ServiceNow (SNOW) tickets.
why_this_course: Network and load balancer teams are asked for traffic flow diagrams all the time: for change reviews, audits, incident bridges and application onboarding. In most teams the answer is a manual exercise of running ping and traceroute, reading the output, and drawing boxes in a diagram tool. The result has no link to the evidence, no timestamp, and goes stale the next time a route or pool member changes. Ping and traceroute are also easy to misread: hops that do not answer, routers that rate-limit ICMP, ECMP paths that create false loops, and load balancers that hide what is behind a VIP all show up in real output [c3] [c4] [c14].

The client asked for automation of this flow with Claude, starting from traceroute and ping access. This course treats Claude as a planner, reader and drafter, not as a probe. Deterministic Python runs the probes and returns typed records; read-only adapters add context from F5, NetScaler, Radware Alteon, other load balancers and Cisco ACI; Claude summarizes and drafts a Mermaid diagram where every node cites its evidence; and a named person approves before anything reaches ServiceNow or a shared repository [c18] [c19] [c21].

The result is a pipeline the team can run on every diagram request and on a schedule, with an audit trail a reviewer can follow. Learners leave with code, tests, a guardrail layer and a runbook they can adapt to their own estate, plus a clear understanding of what a probe-based diagram can and cannot prove.

design_decisions.decision: Start with probe limits before any automation.
design_decisions.rationale: The client input is 'with the help of traceroute and ping access'. Automating misread output only produces wrong diagrams faster, so Module 1 teaches what ICMP, TTL expiry and probe types actually show, and every later module carries the 'unknown, not guessed' rule [c1] [c2] [c3].

design_decisions.decision: Claude never gets a shell; probes run in deterministic code behind narrow MCP tools.
design_decisions.rationale: Probing production networks from an agent with a shell is unsafe and unauditable. Custom tools with fixed schemas, tools=[] in the SDK and a denied Bash tool in Claude Code keep Claude to read-only probes, while hooks enforce scope [c15] [c18] [c20].

design_decisions.decision: Enrich from the load balancers and ACI the client already runs.
design_decisions.rationale: The client's other use cases name F5, NetScaler, Radware and Anaya LB, and Cisco ACI. Traceroute stops at a VIP and cannot see pool members or fabric placement, so read-only API adapters fill those gaps with evidence [c25] [c28] [c30] [c31].

design_decisions.decision: Mermaid as the diagram source of truth.
design_decisions.rationale: Mermaid is text, diffs cleanly in Git, renders natively in GitHub pull requests and can be validated by a command-line renderer, which makes drift detection and review practical. draw.io and Graphviz remain export options [c5] [c6] [c7] [c8] [c37].

design_decisions.decision: Publish through ServiceNow and GitHub behind a named approval.
design_decisions.rationale: Diagram requests arrive as tickets in ServiceNow in the client's environment, and teams keep diagrams in repositories. Writing the result back to the requesting record and to a reviewed pull request fits existing change practice [c39] [c40] [c42].

design_decisions.decision: Add scheduled drift detection with a deterministic diff.
design_decisions.rationale: The core complaint is that diagrams go stale. A scheduled job that re-probes within scope and opens a pull request only on a confirmed change keeps diagrams current without noise; Claude explains, code decides [c43] [c44].

modules.title: What a flow diagram must prove, and what probes can tell you
modules.goal: Set the evidence standard for a traffic diagram and show exactly which parts of a path ping and traceroute can and cannot prove.
learning_objectives: Learners can explain how TTL-based traceroute discovers hops and which ICMP messages it relies on.
Learners can list at least five reasons a hop shows as * or a path looks wrong, including filtering, rate limiting, ECMP and MPLS.
Learners can distinguish forward-path evidence from return-path assumptions.
Learners can state the course operating pattern: Claude plans and explains, code probes, a person approves, everything is logged.
Learners can write a one-page pipeline brief with scope, inputs, outputs and known evidence gaps.

lessons.title: Why diagrams go stale
points: Walk the typical request-to-diagram cycle: a ticket asks for 'the flow from branch to the payments VIP', an engineer runs traceroute and ping, draws boxes in a drawing tool, and the result is never re-checked.
Show the cost: a diagram with no timestamp or probe reference cannot be trusted in a change review or an incident bridge.
Define the course evidence rule: every node and edge must point to a probe record or a device API record, and anything else is labeled unknown.
Frame what Claude adds: planning which probes to run, reading raw output, explaining gaps, and drafting the diagram, while deterministic code does the probing.
Classic traceroute needs about 2n probes for n hops and the path can change during the trace; RFC 1393 tried to fix this with an IP option that never became common, so we live with the limits [c1].

lessons.title: How ping and traceroute actually work
points: ping sends ICMP Echo (type 8) and expects Echo Reply (type 0); the identifier and sequence fields match replies to requests [c2].
Each traceroute probe has a growing TTL; a router that decrements TTL to zero returns ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11, code 0) [c2].
Linux and Cisco IOS default to UDP probes starting at port 33434; the destination answers with ICMP Port Unreachable (type 3 code 3); Windows tracert uses ICMP Echo instead [c3].
Linux traceroute can also probe with ICMP (-I) or TCP SYN (-T, default port 80), which matters when firewalls filter UDP or ICMP [c10].
Default limits to remember: 30 hops, 3 probes per hop on Linux, a 5 second wait on Linux and 4000 ms on Windows [c10] [c12].
Output annotations such as !H, !N, !P and !X tell you the probe was rejected, which is evidence in itself [c10].

lessons.title: Where evidence goes dark
points: Firewalls that drop ICMP or UDP make traceroute stop at the firewall; the hop after is not missing, it is unseen [c10].
Routers rate-limit ICMP; Cisco limits unreachables to one per 500 ms by default, so a final-hop * can be an artifact [c3].
Loss at an intermediate hop does not mean forwarded traffic is lost; mtr's own documentation warns about this [c4].
ECMP and per-flow load balancing create false loops and diamonds unless the probe header is held constant (Paris traceroute approach) [c14].
MPLS cores may hide hops or show them only if routers append the label stack per RFC 4950 [c13].
Load balancers terminate or proxy connections, so traceroute to a VIP shows the VIP, never the pool members behind it; that context must come from the device API (Module 5).
Traceroute only shows the forward path from the source; the return path can differ and must be marked as not observed.

lessons.title: The course pattern and the pipeline brief
points: Claude plans and explains; Python code runs the probes; device adapters read state; a named person approves publication; every step is logged.
Claude never receives a shell tool in this course; it gets narrow, read-only tools only (Module 2).
The pipeline brief records: requester, source, target, protocol and port of interest, allowed prefixes, probe budget, devices to enrich from, and where the result is published.
The brief also lists known blind spots for the target path, such as firewalls that drop ICMP or an MPLS core.
The capstone acceptance test is derived from this brief, so it must be specific.

Run mtr --report for 20 cycles and point out loss at an intermediate hop that does not appear at the destination [c4].

Write the hop table on a whiteboard with columns: hop, address, RTTs, evidence type, confidence, notes.

lab.brief: Trace the path from the lab client to the lab payments VIP by hand, record every hop and every gap, and write the brief for the pipeline you will build.
steps: Log in to the lab client and confirm the target VIP and allowed prefix list from the lab handout.
Run ping -c 10 -W 2 to the VIP and record loss and average RTT [c11].
Run traceroute -n -q 3 -w 2 -m 30 to the VIP and save raw output to a text file with a timestamp [c10].
Repeat with -I and with -T -p 443 and save both outputs.
Run mtr --report -c 20 and save the report [c4].
Fill in the hop table: for each hop note address, RTTs, which probe types answered and a confidence of high, medium or unknown.
Mark every gap and write the most likely reason (filtering, rate limiting, ECMP, MPLS, load balancer).
Write a one-page pipeline brief using the course template, including scope, budget, enrichment sources and publication targets.
success_criteria: All raw outputs are saved with timestamps and the command used.
Every hop in the table has a confidence value and every * has a stated likely reason.
The brief names allowed prefixes, probe budget, enrichment devices and an approver role.
The learner can explain why pool members do not appear in the trace.

common_pitfalls: Treating a * hop as a broken link rather than a router that did not answer.
Reading intermediate-hop loss in mtr as packet loss on the forwarded path [c4].
Assuming the return path matches the forward path.
Running traceroute with name resolution on and blaming slow DNS for slow hops; use -n or /d [c10] [c12].
Forgetting that Windows and Linux use different probe protocols by default, so results differ through the same firewall [c3].

knowledge_check.q: Which ICMP message does a router send when a traceroute probe's TTL expires?
knowledge_check.a: ICMP Time Exceeded, type 11, code 0 [c2].

knowledge_check.q: Why might traceroute show a diamond or loop that does not exist?
knowledge_check.a: Per-flow load balancing (ECMP) sends probes with different header fields down different paths; holding the flow fields constant avoids it [c14].

knowledge_check.q: Why does a trace to a load balancer VIP never show the pool members?
knowledge_check.a: The load balancer owns the VIP and proxies or translates traffic to members, so probes terminate at the VIP; member context must come from the device API.

knowledge_check.q: What does a final hop of * * * mean on a Cisco-routed path?
knowledge_check.a: Possibly that ICMP unreachables are rate limited (one per 500 ms by default) or filtered, not that the target is down [c3].

modules.title: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP for this workflow
modules.goal: Build a Claude workbench where Claude can call read-only probe tools and nothing else, with credentials kept out of prompts.
learning_objectives: Learners can write a CLAUDE.md and a .claude/settings.json that set project conventions and permission rules.
Learners can define custom tools in the Python Agent SDK and restrict Claude to those tools only.
Learners can register a stdio MCP server with Claude Code at project scope.
Learners can add a PreToolUse hook that blocks out-of-scope calls and a PostToolUse hook that logs every call.
Learners can keep device tokens in environment variables or a vault and out of the model context.

lessons.title: Claude Code project layout
points: Repository layout: probes/ (runners), adapters/ (devices), schema/ (Pydantic models), diagrams/ (published .mmd), evidence/ (bundles), mcp_server/, tests/, and CLAUDE.md.
CLAUDE.md lives at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, is shared through Git, and can be started with /init [c16].
Teach clearly that CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement; anything that must be blocked goes in permission rules or hooks [c16].
Permission rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins, so a broad deny cannot be undone by a narrow allow [c15].
Put Bash in deny for the probe agent so the tool is removed from Claude's context entirely, and allow only mcp__probe__* [c15].
Remind learners that Bash rules match command text and are not a security boundary; the real control is not giving Claude a shell [c15].

lessons.title: Agent SDK sessions and custom tools
points: Define tools with the @tool decorator: name, description, input schema and an async handler that returns content [c18].
Wrap tools with create_sdk_mcp_server(name='probe', version='1.0.0', tools=[...]) and pass it in mcp_servers [c18].
Set tools=[] so all built-in tools are removed and Claude can only use your MCP tools; list each tool as mcp__probe__<name> in allowed_tools [c18].
Use a full JSON Schema input with enums and ranges, for example count 1 to 10 and timeout 1 to 5 seconds, so bad arguments fail validation [c18].
Return is_error with a composed message when a probe fails so Claude can react sensibly instead of seeing a raw exception [c18].
Mark probe tools with readOnlyHint, but explain this is metadata only and does not enforce anything [c18].

lessons.title: The read-only probe MCP server
points: Expose three tools only: ping, traceroute and dns_lookup; each wraps the deterministic runner from Module 3.
MCP clients discover tools with tools/list and call them with tools/call; results carry content, structuredContent and isError [c21].
The MCP specification says servers MUST validate inputs, implement access controls, rate limit invocations and sanitize outputs; clients SHOULD log tool usage and use timeouts [c21].
Register the server with claude mcp add --scope project probe -- python -m mcp_server; project scope writes .mcp.json and prompts for approval the first time [c17].
Every tool call writes an audit line: timestamp, tool, arguments, caller session, result status and probe ID.

lessons.title: Hooks and secrets
points: A PreToolUse hook with HookMatcher(matcher='^mcp__probe__') checks tool_input['target'] against the scope list and returns permissionDecision 'deny' with a reason [c20].
Matchers match tool names only, so argument checks must happen inside the hook body [c20].
A PostToolUse hook appends to the audit log; if hooks disagree, deny wins [c20].
Device API tokens are read by the adapter from environment variables or a vault at call time and never appear in tool arguments, results or prompts.
Add Read deny rules for .env and secrets/** so Claude Code cannot open them through file tools [c15].

instructor_demo: Show the repository tree and the CLAUDE.md with probe conventions and the evidence rule.
Open .claude/settings.json with deny: ['Bash'] and allow: ['mcp__probe__*'] and explain evaluation order [c15].
Run claude mcp add --scope project probe -- python -m mcp_server and show the generated .mcp.json [c17].
Start an Agent SDK script with tools=[] and the probe server, and ask Claude to trace the lab VIP [c18].
Ask Claude to run 'ls /' and show it has no tool to do so.
Ask Claude to ping 8.8.8.8 and show the PreToolUse hook denying it with a reason [c20].
Open the audit log and show one line per tool call.

lab.brief: Stand up the MCP server, connect it to Claude Code and the Agent SDK, and prove Claude can call a probe tool but cannot run an arbitrary shell command.
steps: Clone the course repository and create a Python virtual environment with the pinned requirements.
Write CLAUDE.md with the evidence rule, repository layout and test command.
Create .claude/settings.json with Bash denied, Read deny rules for secrets, and the probe tools allowed.
Implement the MCP server with ping, traceroute and dns_lookup tools calling stub runners.
Register the server at project scope and confirm Claude Code lists the tools.
Write an Agent SDK script with tools=[], the in-process probe server and a PreToolUse scope hook.
Ask Claude to trace an in-scope target, an out-of-scope target and to run a shell command; record what happens.
Inspect the audit log for all three attempts.
success_criteria: Claude successfully calls the in-scope probe and returns its result.
The out-of-scope probe is denied by the hook with a logged reason.
No shell command runs, and the transcript shows Claude had no shell tool.
No credential appears in any prompt, tool argument or log line.

common_pitfalls: Relying on CLAUDE.md text to prevent shell use instead of removing the tool [c16].
Adding an allow rule and expecting it to override a broader deny [c15].
Writing a hook matcher that tries to match a target IP; matchers only see tool names [c20].
Forgetting that a project-scoped MCP server needs approval on first use, then assuming it is broken [c17].
Passing device passwords as tool arguments so they end up in transcripts.

knowledge_check.q: A deny rule says Bash and an allow rule says Bash(traceroute *). Can Claude run traceroute through Bash?
knowledge_check.a: No. Deny is evaluated first and a bare Bash deny removes the tool from context [c15].

knowledge_check.q: How do you make sure the Agent SDK session has no built-in tools at all?
knowledge_check.a: Pass tools=[] so only your MCP tools remain [c18].

knowledge_check.q: Where should an argument-level scope check live?
knowledge_check.a: Inside a PreToolUse hook body (and in the tool handler), because matchers only match tool names [c20].

knowledge_check.q: Name two duties the MCP specification places on servers.
knowledge_check.a: Any two of: validate inputs, implement access controls, rate limit invocations, sanitize outputs [c21].

modules.title: Deterministic probe runners in Python
modules.goal: Wrap ping and traceroute in tested Python runners that always return a typed record, whatever the network does.
learning_objectives: Learners can call ping and traceroute through subprocess with timeouts, fixed argument lists and exit-code handling.
Learners can parse Linux and Windows output into one typed hop list.
Learners can handle stars, duplicate hops, annotations and partial paths without guessing.
Learners can unit test parsers against saved captures.
Learners can expose runners to Claude as tools that return structured results.

lessons.title: Running probes safely
points: Build the command as a list, never a shell string, and validate the target as an IP or allowed hostname before building it.
Use subprocess.run(..., timeout=N, capture_output=True); on timeout the child is killed and TimeoutExpired is raised, which the runner turns into a failed record [c22].
ping exit codes: 0 success, 1 no replies (or fewer than count by deadline), 2 other error; record the code rather than treating non-zero as a crash [c11].
Fix probe parameters per run: ping -c 5 -W 2 -w 15; traceroute -n -q 3 -w 2 -m 30 [c10] [c11].
Record the tool version (traceroute -V, ping -V) and the exact command in every record.

lessons.title: Parsing Linux and Windows output
points: Linux traceroute prints a hop number, then per-probe address and RTT or *; annotations such as !H or !X follow the RTT [c10].
Windows tracert prints three RTT columns then an address; 'Request timed out' rows are all asterisks [c12].
Normalize both into Hop(ttl, responders[], rtts_ms[], annotations[], status) with status of answered, partial or no_reply.
A hop can have several responders when probes take different ECMP paths; keep them all rather than picking one [c14].
Save each raw capture next to its parsed record so a reviewer can replay the parse.

lessons.title: The ugly cases
points: Stars: record no_reply with zero responders; never interpolate an address.
Duplicate addresses on consecutive hops can mean a router decrementing TTL oddly or a load balancer; flag them, do not merge them.
Rate-limited routers: with many simultaneous probes (default 16 on Linux) some routers throttle ICMP, so lower -N for consistent output [c10].
Partially answering paths: the destination may answer even when middle hops do not; mark reached_target independently of hop completeness.
Destination unreachable annotations are evidence of filtering and should be kept as such [c10].

lessons.title: Tests and tool exposure
points: Build a fixtures folder of captures: clean path, firewall-dark hop, rate-limited final hop, ECMP split, Windows output.
Write pytest cases asserting hop count, statuses and RTT values for each capture.
Validate the parsed result with Pydantic model_validate so a parser bug fails loudly with ValidationError [c24].
The MCP tool handler calls the runner and returns the record as JSON content; on failure it returns is_error with a clear message [c18].
Claude requests a probe, code runs it, Claude receives only the structured record and the probe ID.

instructor_demo: Open a raw Linux capture with a * hop and a !X annotation and walk through the parser.
Run the runner against a black-hole lab target and show TimeoutExpired being turned into a failed record [c22].
Show ping returning exit 1 for an unreachable target and the record capturing it [c11].
Parse a Windows tracert capture into the same record type [c12].
Ask Claude Code to add a parser test for a new capture, then review the diff line by line before accepting.
Call the probe tool from Claude and show the structured JSON that comes back.

lab.brief: Implement and test the probe runners with Claude Code, inspect every diff, and run them against three lab targets with different failure modes.
steps: Review the provided capture fixtures and expected results.
Ask Claude Code to draft the ping runner with timeout and exit-code handling; review and correct the diff.
Draft the Linux traceroute parser and run the tests against the fixtures.
Add the Windows tracert parser and its tests.
Add handling for stars, duplicate hops, annotations and multiple responders.
Connect the runners to the MCP tools from Module 2.
Run probes against target A (clean), target B (behind a firewall dropping ICMP) and target C (rate-limited).
Compare the three records and note what each status means.
success_criteria: All parser tests pass, including the ugly cases.
No runner path uses shell=True or string-built commands.
A timeout produces a failed record, not an unhandled exception.
The three lab targets produce three distinct, correctly labeled records.

common_pitfalls: Building commands with f-strings and shell=True, opening an injection path.
Treating ping exit code 1 as a crash rather than a valid 'no reply' result [c11].
Collapsing multiple responders on one hop into a single address [c14].
Accepting Claude-drafted parsers without running them against real captures.
Leaving default 16 parallel probes and getting inconsistent results from throttled routers [c10].

knowledge_check.q: What happens to the child process when subprocess.run times out?
knowledge_check.a: It is killed and waited for, then TimeoutExpired is raised [c22].

knowledge_check.q: Which ping exit code means no replies were received?
knowledge_check.a: 1; 2 means another error [c11].

knowledge_check.q: What is the default wait per traceroute probe on Windows?
knowledge_check.a: 4000 ms, set with /w [c12].

knowledge_check.q: Why keep multiple responders for a single TTL?
knowledge_check.a: They show ECMP or load balancing, which a single address would hide [c14].

modules.title: Path evidence model and structured outputs
modules.goal: Define the path record and evidence bundle, and make Claude summarize a path with mandatory probe citations and no invented hops.
learning_objectives: Learners can write a Pydantic schema for a path record with explicit unknown segments and per-hop confidence.
Learners can produce JSON Schema from the model and use it as an Agent SDK output format.
Learners can prompt Claude to cite probe IDs for every claim and to refuse to fill gaps.
Learners can lay out a versioned evidence bundle that a reviewer can replay.

lessons.title: The path record schema
points: Fields: path_id, source, target, protocol, port, started_at, finished_at, probe_ids[], tool_versions, hops[], reached_target, notes.
Hop fields: ttl, responders[], rtts_ms[], loss_pct, status (answered, partial, no_reply), confidence (high, medium, unknown), evidence_refs[].
Unknown segments are first-class objects: from_hop, to_hop, reason (filtered, rate_limited, mpls, lb, unknown), never a guessed address.

points: Log in with POST /api/aaaLogin.json and an aaaUser name and password; reuse the APIC-cookie token [c31].

lessons.title: Hybrid and cloud paths

Cloud lookups use read-only roles and are tools like any other, logged with evidence IDs.

lessons.title: What to enrich and what to leave unknown
points: Enrich when a read-only API can answer with a timestamped fact; leave unknown when the only source would be a guess or a stale document.
Never enrich from memory or from Claude's general knowledge of typical designs.
Write the enrichment decision into the evidence bundle so the reviewer can see why a segment is unknown.
Agree the enrichment policy with the approver role in advance.

modules.title: Guardrails, approvals and audit for probing and publishing
modules.goal: Enforce scope, rate limits, approvals and audit in code so the pipeline is safe on production networks.
learning_objectives: Learners can enforce a prefix and hostname scope list in code at more than one layer.
Learners can implement per-target and per-hour probe budgets.
Learners can require a named approver before any write to ServiceNow or a shared repository.

lessons.title: Scope lists in code
points: Scope file lists allowed prefixes and hostnames; resolve hostnames first and check every resolved address.
Enforce in three places: the PreToolUse hook, the MCP tool handler and the runner itself [c20] [c21].
The prompt may mention scope for clarity, but scope is never enforced by the prompt.
Out-of-scope requests return a denial with a reason and are logged [c20].

lessons.title: Rate limits and probe budgets
points: The MCP specification requires servers to rate limit tool invocations [c21].
Budget example: 50 probes per hour per pipeline, 3 per target per run, at most 2 concurrent runs.
Lower traceroute parallelism (-N) to avoid triggering ICMP throttling on routers [c10].
When the budget is exhausted, the tool returns is_error with 'budget exhausted' and Claude must report it [c18].

lessons.title: Approval gate
points: Publishing tools are separate from probing tools and are not given to the drafting agent.
The publish step checks the approval record: approver name, role, time, request ID and the hash of the bundle approved.
If the bundle hash changes after approval, the approval is void.
MCP clients should present confirmation for sensitive operations and keep a human able to deny invocations [c21].

lessons.title: Audit log
points: Log every tool call, device query, model output hash and approval decision as JSON lines.
PostToolUse hooks write the tool call side; adapters write the device side [c20].
Store logs append-only and outside the repository; ship to the SIEM if the customer has one.
The audit export for a request is attached to the change record in Module 9.

modules.title: Drift detection and scheduled re-mapping
modules.goal: Re-run in-scope probes on a schedule, detect real path changes deterministically, and raise a pull request with Claude's explanation only when something changed.
learning_objectives: Learners can write a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow and understand its timing limits.
Learners can diff two path records deterministically and classify changes.
Learners can have Claude explain a diff in plain language with structured output.
Learners can write an operator runbook for false drift.

lessons.title: Scheduling the job
points: on: schedule with cron '21 21 * * *' runs at 21:21 UTC (02:51 IST); cron is UTC unless a timezone is set [c43].
Runs use the default branch, the minimum interval is 5 minutes, and runs can be delayed or dropped at busy times such as the top of the hour, so avoid minute 0 [c43].
Public repositories disable scheduled workflows after 60 days without activity [c43].
The runner must sit inside the network that can reach the targets, so use a self-hosted runner in the lab network.
Probes still pass through the same scope list and budget as the interactive pipeline.

lessons.title: Deterministic diff
points: Compare hop sequences by responder sets, not single addresses, to avoid ECMP noise [c14].
Classify: new hop, removed hop, changed responder, newly unknown, newly answering, VIP member change.
Ignore RTT changes below a threshold; RTT is not path.
Require two consecutive runs to agree before raising drift, to filter one-off probe failures.

lessons.title: Claude explains the change
points: Feed the diff and both records to Claude with a structured output schema: summary, changes[{type, hops, evidence_refs}], likely_causes[], confidence [c19].
Claude must cite probe IDs for both the old and new state.
The diff decides whether a PR is opened; Claude only explains.
The PR body contains the diff, Claude's explanation and links to the bundles [c42].

lessons.title: Pull requests from automation and the runbook
points: A PR opened with GITHUB_TOKEN creates pull_request runs in an approval-required state, so a person must approve CI on drift PRs [c44].
Grant only contents: write and pull-requests: write to the job.
Runbook: ECMP flapping, maintenance windows, probe failures, firewall changes that hide hops, and how to suppress a known false drift.
Close stale drift PRs automatically if the path returns to the published state.

modules.title: Capstone: request to approved flow diagram, end to end
modules.goal: Run the full pipeline from a ServiceNow request to an approved, published and monitored diagram, and defend it to the group.
learning_objectives: Learners can run the full pipeline across probes, enrichment, diagram, approval and publication.

lessons.title: Capstone scenario
points: A ServiceNow request asks for the payments flow from a branch client to the payments VIP at the lab data center.
The path crosses a firewall that drops ICMP, an F5 or NetScaler VIP, an Alteon or Anaya LB segment through the common adapter, and the ACI fabric.
Teams must produce the diagram, bundle, PR, ServiceNow update and drift job.
The instructor injects one surprise: a pool member change or a new hop mid-exercise.

lessons.title: Acceptance and limitations
points: Acceptance criteria come from the Module 1 brief and the guardrail rules.
The limitations statement lists each unknown segment and why it is unknown.
Return path is stated as not observed unless separately probed from the far side.
Every claim in the demo must be backed by an evidence ID.

lessons.title: Review and demo
points: Peer review uses the audit log, not the code.
Demo: request in, probes, enrichment, diagram, approval, publication, drift check.
Reviewers try one out-of-scope probe and one unapproved publish.
Teams close with what they would change before production.

instructor_demo: Brief the scenario and show the acceptance checklist.
Show a reference run end to end in under ten minutes.
Inject the surprise change after teams publish their first version.
Model a good review by asking for evidence behind two nodes.

steps: Submit the capstone request in ServiceNow.
Run probes and enrichment for all segments.
Generate, check and render the diagram.
Obtain approval from the designated approver.
Publish to ServiceNow and GitHub.
Run the drift job after the injected change and handle the PR.
Present the demo and limitations statement.
success_criteria: Every node in the final diagram has valid evidence.
No publish occurred without approval, shown in the audit log.
The injected change is detected and explained.
The limitations statement is accurate and complete.

Manually fixing a node in the diagram to save time.
Approving your own team's publish.

capstone_plan.brief: Teams build a repeatable pipeline that takes a flow diagram request from ServiceNow, runs ping and traceroute through deterministic code, enriches hops from load balancer and ACI APIs, has Claude draft an evidence-linked Mermaid diagram, and publishes to ServiceNow and GitHub only after a named approval, with drift detection on a schedule.

Probes run within scope and budget; path record saved.
Enrichment complete across load balancers and ACI, with unknowns labeled.
Approval recorded against the bundle hash.
Published to ServiceNow and GitHub; PR merged.
Drift job detects and explains the injected change.
evaluation_notes: Score evidence integrity first: any node without valid evidence fails the capstone.
Check the audit log for approval-before-publish and refused out-of-scope probes.
Assess the limitations statement for accuracy, including the return path.
Assess clarity of Claude's summary and drift explanation for a non-specialist approver.
Assess code quality: tests on parsers and adapters, no shell=True, credentials handled correctly.

promo_video_research.hook_basis: The opening scenario (a ticket asks for the flow to a payments VIP, an engineer runs traceroute and ping and draws by hand, and the path changes) is a teaching scenario, but it is grounded in documented behavior: traceroute paths can change during and between traces, and load balancing creates path artifacts [c1] [c14].

F5, NetScaler, Radware Alteon and Cisco ACI, each with a documented read API [c25] [c28] [c30] [c31]. Anaya LB is covered through the common adapter; no public Anaya LB API documentation was found, so it is taught with mocked or customer-provided interfaces.
A design rule enforced by the evidence checker in the diagram module, not an external fact.

claims_check.basis: Consistent with iControl REST virtual (destination, pool) and pool members resources [c25] [c26]; names and addresses are fictional.

Rendering and parsing with mermaid-cli and mermaid.parse are real validation steps [c36] [c37]; 'lint' here means the course evidence checker.

claims_check.basis: Design rule enforced by the schema's explicit unknown segments and the citation checker; supported by documented reasons hops do not answer [c3] [c4] [c10].

citations.title: RFC 1393: Traceroute Using an IP Option
citations.supports: Module 1: why classic traceroute needs many probes and can see a changing path
citations.key_fact: Classic TTL-based traceroute generates about 2n packets for n hops; RFC 1393 proposed an IP Traceroute option and ICMP Traceroute message (type 30) so the path is logged with n+1 packets and does not suffer from a changing path. It is Experimental and obsoleted by RFC 6814 (the RFC Editor header now shows it as Historic).

citations.title: RFC 792: Internet Control Message Protocol
citations.supports: Module 1: ICMP Echo, Echo Reply and Time Exceeded
citations.key_fact: ICMP Echo is type 8 and Echo Reply type 0, with identifier and sequence number fields to match replies to requests and the data echoed back unchanged; Time Exceeded is type 11, code 0 meaning time to live exceeded in transit.

citations.title: Use the Traceroute Command on Operating Systems
citations.supports: Module 1 and 3: probe behavior on Cisco IOS, Linux and Windows
citations.key_fact: Cisco IOS and Linux traceroute send UDP probes starting at destination port 33434 with TTL 1 (default maximum 30 hops); hops return ICMP Time Exceeded and the destination returns ICMP Port Unreachable (type 3 code 3). Windows tracert uses ICMP Echo. Cisco routers rate-limit ICMP unreachables to one per 500 ms by default, which can show as asterisks for the final hop.

citations.title: mtr: Official repository for mtr, a network diagnostic tool
citations.supports: Module 1 and 3: continuous per-hop statistics and the meaning of intermediate-hop loss
citations.key_fact: mtr combines traceroute and ping, sends probes with increasing TTL and prints running per-hop statistics; routers may never send or may rate-limit ICMP responses, so apparent loss at an intermediate hop does not always mean forwarded traffic is lost there.

citations.title: Flowcharts Syntax | Mermaid
citations.supports: Module 7: Mermaid flowchart syntax, subgraphs, shapes and classDef styling
citations.key_fact: Flowcharts start with flowchart (or graph) plus a direction (TB/TD, BT, RL, LR); links include -->, ---, dotted -.- and thick ===; subgraph id [Title] ... end groups nodes; from v11.3.0 shapes can be set with A@{ shape: ... }; classDef defines a reusable style applied with class; a lowercase end inside a node label breaks the diagram; commas in stroke-dasharray must be escaped.

citations.title: Creating diagrams - GitHub Docs
citations.supports: Module 7 and 9: rendering Mermaid in GitHub pull requests and Markdown files
citations.key_fact: GitHub renders Mermaid from a fenced code block labeled mermaid in issues, discussions, pull requests, wikis and Markdown files; a mermaid block containing info reveals which Mermaid version GitHub runs.

citations.title: Insert a diagram from specially formatted CSV data | draw.io
citations.supports: Module 7: optional draw.io export for teams that maintain diagrams in draw.io
citations.key_fact: Arrange > Insert > Advanced > CSV takes # configuration lines before the CSV data; # label: uses %column% placeholders, # connect: takes a JSON object with from/to columns, # identity: lets a re-import update existing shapes instead of duplicating them, and # layout: auto applies an automatic layout.

citations.title: DOT Language | Graphviz
citations.supports: Module 7: Graphviz DOT as an alternative renderer
citations.key_fact: DOT declares graph (edges --) or digraph (edges ->), optionally strict to forbid multi-edges; attributes are key=value pairs in brackets; graph/node/edge statements set defaults for objects defined afterwards; subgraphs named cluster* are drawn in a bounding box where the layout engine supports it.

citations.title: Prompting best practices
citations.supports: Module 4 and 7: prompting Claude for evidence-cited summaries and clean diagram output
citations.key_fact: Tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do, wrap instructions, context and input in XML tags to reduce misinterpretation, and use structured outputs or tool calling for fixed structure; examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer output format and structure.

citations.title: traceroute(8) - Linux manual page
citations.supports: Module 1 and 3: Linux traceroute options, methods and output annotations
citations.key_fact: Options include -I (ICMP ECHO probes), -T (TCP SYN probes, default destination port 80, intended to get past firewalls), -m max_ttl (default 30), -q nqueries (default 3 probes per hop), -w wait (default max 5.0 s), -N simultaneous probes (default 16; routers may throttle ICMP) and -n. The default method uses UDP to unlikely ports starting at 33434. No response prints *, and annotations such as !H, !N, !P and !X mark host, network, protocol unreachable and administratively prohibited.

citations.title: ping(8) - Linux manual page
citations.supports: Module 3: ping options and exit codes for deterministic wrappers
citations.key_fact: -c count stops after count ECHO_REQUESTs, -W timeout sets the per-reply wait in seconds, -w deadline sets an overall timeout; ping exits 1 if no reply is received (or fewer than count by the deadline), 2 on other errors, and 0 otherwise.

citations.title: tracert | Microsoft Learn
citations.supports: Module 3: Windows tracert syntax and output for the Windows parser
citations.key_fact: Syntax tracert [/d] [/h <maximumhops>] [/j <hostlist>] [/w <timeout>] [/R] [/S <srcaddr>] [/4][/6] <targetname>; /d skips name resolution, /h default is 30 hops, /w default is 4000 ms and an asterisk is printed when no reply arrives in time; routers that do not return Time Exceeded show as a row of asterisks; pathping gives per-hop loss.

citations.title: RFC 4950: ICMP Extensions for Multiprotocol Label Switching
citations.supports: Module 1: MPLS hops and what traceroute can show inside an MPLS core
citations.key_fact: Defines an ICMP extension object that lets Label Switching Routers append the MPLS label stack to ICMP messages so enhanced traceroute can show MPLS information; an LSR that cannot deliver a labeled datagram removes the label stack and generates the ICMP message from the inner IP datagram.

citations.title: Detection, Understanding, and Prevention of Traceroute Measurement Artifacts
citations.supports: Module 1 and 10: ECMP and load balancing artifacts in traceroute
citations.key_fact: Load balancing routers cause false loops, cycles and diamonds in traceroute output; Paris traceroute controls packet header contents so probes follow one path and gives a truer picture of the routes packets take.

citations.title: Configure permissions - Claude Code Docs
citations.supports: Module 2 and 8: allow, ask and deny rules for Bash and MCP tools
citations.key_fact: Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins regardless of specificity; a bare tool name such as Bash in deny removes the tool from context; mcp__<server>__* matches every tool from one server; Bash rules match command text and are not a security boundary around a program, so pair them with the sandbox when a restriction must hold; project rules live in .claude/settings.json.

citations.title: How Claude remembers your project - Claude Code Docs
citations.supports: Module 2: CLAUDE.md conventions for the pipeline repository
citations.key_fact: Project instructions live in ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md and are shared through version control; /init generates a starting CLAUDE.md; Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration, so use a PreToolUse hook to block an action.

citations.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP - Claude Code Docs
citations.supports: Module 2: registering the probe MCP server with Claude Code
citations.key_fact: Stdio servers are added with claude mcp add [options] <name> -- <command> [args...]; scopes are local (default), project (stored in .mcp.json at the project root and shared via version control) and user; interactive sessions ask for approval before using project-scoped servers.

citations.title: Give Claude custom tools - Claude Agent SDK
citations.supports: Module 2, 3 and 5: defining probe and device tools in the Python Agent SDK
citations.key_fact: Python tools use the @tool decorator (name, description, input schema, async handler) and are wrapped with create_sdk_mcp_server; tools are named mcp__{server}__{tool} and listed in allowed_tools; tools=[] removes all built-in tools so Claude can only use your MCP tools; a bare name in disallowed_tools removes a built-in from context; readOnlyHint annotations are metadata, not enforcement; handlers return content and optionally is_error.

citations.title: Get structured output from agents - Claude Agent SDK
citations.supports: Module 4 and 10: schema-validated summaries and drift explanations
citations.key_fact: Pass output_format={'type': 'json_schema', 'schema': ...} (Pydantic model_json_schema() works) and read ResultMessage.structured_output; the SDK validates with JSON Schema draft-07 and re-prompts on mismatch; failure ends with subtype error_max_structured_output_retries, and a success result without structured_output must also be treated as a failure.

citations.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks - Claude Agent SDK
citations.supports: Module 2 and 8: PreToolUse scope checks and PostToolUse audit logging
citations.key_fact: PreToolUse hooks registered with HookMatcher can return hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision 'deny' with a permissionDecisionReason; matchers match tool names (MCP tools as mcp__<server>__<action>), not arguments, so check tool_input inside the hook; when several hooks disagree deny wins; PostToolUse suits audit logging; a timed-out PreToolUse hook blocks the call.

citations.title: Tools - Model Context Protocol specification (2025-06-18)
citations.supports: Module 2 and 8: MCP tool discovery, results and security duties
citations.key_fact: Clients discover tools with tools/list and call them with tools/call; tools carry name, description, inputSchema, optional outputSchema and annotations (untrusted unless from trusted servers); results carry content, structuredContent and isError; servers MUST validate inputs, implement access controls, rate limit invocations and sanitize outputs; clients SHOULD keep a human able to deny invocations, use timeouts and log tool usage for audit.

citations.title: subprocess - Subprocess management
citations.supports: Module 3: timeouts and exit-code handling in probe runners
citations.key_fact: With run(timeout=...), the child is killed and TimeoutExpired is raised after it terminates; CalledProcessError is raised for a non-zero exit when check=True and carries returncode, cmd and captured output.

citations.title: JSON Schema | Pydantic Docs
citations.supports: Module 4: generating the path record schema
citations.key_fact: BaseModel.model_json_schema() returns a jsonable dict of the model's JSON Schema; Pydantic targets JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 and OpenAPI 3.1.0.

citations.title: Models | Pydantic Docs
citations.supports: Module 3 and 4: validating parsed probe output
citations.key_fact: model_validate() validates an object and model_validate_json() validates a JSON string or bytes; ValidationError is raised when data cannot be parsed into a model instance.

citations.title: APIRef_tm_ltm_virtual
citations.supports: Module 5: reading F5 virtual servers
citations.key_fact: The collection /mgmt/tm/ltm/virtual supports OPTIONS and GET; properties include destination (virtual address and port), pool (default pool), ipProtocol and the partition (tmPartition, default Common).

citations.title: APIRef_tm_ltm_pool_members
citations.supports: Module 5: reading F5 pool members and their state
citations.key_fact: Pool members live at /mgmt/tm/ltm/pool/~<pool id>/members; properties include address, state (user-down forces the member offline), session (default user-enabled) and monitor.

citations.title: Demystifying iControl REST Part 3 - How to pass query parameters and tmsh options
citations.supports: Module 5: efficient read-only F5 queries
citations.key_fact: iControl REST supports OData $filter, $select, $skip and $top, plus expandSubcollections (returns subcollections such as pool members in the first request), options (adds tmsh arguments) and ver (pins behavior to a TMOS version); example /mgmt/tm/ltm/pool?$filter=partition+eq+staging&$select=name,loadBalancingMode.

citations.title: lbvserver | configuration (NITRO API)
citations.supports: Module 5: reading NetScaler load balancing virtual servers
citations.key_fact: GET (all) is /nitro/v1/config/lbvserver with attrs and filter query parameters; fields include name, servicetype, ipv46, port and read-only curstate and effectivestate (UP, DOWN, OUT OF SERVICE and others); requests carry Cookie: NITRO_AUTH_TOKEN, or X-NITRO-USER and X-NITRO-PASS headers for single authenticated operations.

citations.title: lbvserver_servicegroup_binding | configuration (NITRO API)
citations.supports: Module 5: mapping a NetScaler vserver to its service groups
citations.key_fact: The binding object /nitro/v1/config/lbvserver_servicegroup_binding links a virtual server name to servicegroupname (with weight and order); add is a PUT and returns 201 Created.

citations.title: alteon-sdk (PyPI project metadata)
citations.publisher: PyPI (package published by a Radware author)
citations.supports: Module 5: Radware Alteon access from Python
citations.key_fact: alteon-sdk provides a Python API to Alteon structures via a REST backend, with beans such as SlbNewCfgEnhRealServerTable read through AlteonClient(...).api.device.read(bean); it requires Python 3.6 or later and lists minimum supported Alteon versions 31.0.10.0 and 32.2.2.0; the latest release on PyPI is a beta (0.16b2).

citations.title: Cisco APIC REST API Configuration Guide, Release 4.2(x) and Later - Using the REST API
citations.supports: Module 6: APIC login, class and managed object queries
citations.key_fact: Log in with POST https://<apic>/api/aaaLogin.json and an aaaUser object; the token is sent back as the APIC-cookie; class queries use /api/class/<className>.json and MO queries /api/mo/<dn>.json; query-target is self, children or subtree (default self), query-target-filter takes expressions such as eq(attribute,value), and rsp-subtree is no, children or full (default no).

citations.title: Cisco Live LTRDCN-3225 ACI programmability lab: class queries and children
citations.supports: Module 6: locating an endpoint on a leaf
citations.key_fact: The children of fvCEp hold the endpoint's location in the fabric, specifically fvRsCEpToPathEp; query /api/node/class/fvCEp.json?rsp-subtree=children&rsp-subtree-class=fvRsCEpToPathEp style requests to include them, because a plain fvCEp query does not return its children.

citations.title: ACI Sandboxes - Cisco DevNet
citations.supports: Lab environment: free APIC access
citations.key_fact: DevNet offers an Always-On ACI Simulator (shared, no reservation) and a reservable ACI Simulator sandbox (up to 5 consecutive days) for REST API work over HTTP/HTTPS with XML and JSON.

citations.title: Configure route tables - Amazon VPC
citations.supports: Module 6: where traceroute stops and VPC route tables begin
citations.key_fact: A route table holds routes that decide where traffic from a subnet or gateway is directed; each route has a destination (CIDR or prefix list) and a target such as an internet gateway, NAT gateway, peering connection or VPN connection; a main route table is created with every VPC.

citations.title: Next hop overview - Azure Network Watcher
citations.supports: Module 6: Azure next hop as cloud path evidence
citations.key_fact: Next hop returns the next hop type, IP address and route table ID for a destination; types include Internet, VirtualAppliance, VirtualNetworkGateway, VirtualNetwork, VirtualNetworkPeering, VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint, MicrosoftEdge and None; System Route is returned when no user-defined route applies.

citations.title: Usage | Mermaid
citations.supports: Module 7: validating Mermaid without rendering, and security level
citations.key_fact: mermaid.parse(text, parseOptions) checks a definition without rendering; it returns an object with diagramType when valid and throws (or returns false with suppressErrors) when invalid; securityLevel strict (default) encodes HTML tags and disables click functionality.

citations.title: mermaid-cli
citations.supports: Module 7: deterministic command-line rendering
citations.key_fact: Install with npm install -g @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli and run mmdc -i input.mmd -o output.svg to produce SVG, PNG or PDF; a Docker image is published as minlag/mermaid-cli.

citations.title: Sequence diagrams | Mermaid
citations.supports: Module 7: request-response flow diagrams
citations.key_fact: sequenceDiagram declares participant and actor lines (with aliases), solid ->> and dashed -->> messages, activate/deactivate, autonumber and Note over A,B for annotations.

citations.title: Table API (Zurich release)
citations.supports: Module 9: updating the requesting record
citations.key_fact: Endpoints are GET/POST /now/table/{tableName} and GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /now/table/{tableName}/{sys_id}; sysparm_query is an encoded query, sysparm_fields limits returned fields, sysparm_limit caps records (default 10000).

citations.title: Attachment API (Xanadu release)
citations.supports: Module 9: attaching the diagram and evidence bundle
citations.key_fact: POST /now/attachment/file uploads a binary file with required query parameters table_name, table_sys_id and file_name; POST /now/attachment/upload takes multipart form data; GET /now/attachment/{sys_id}/file returns the file.

citations.title: REST API endpoints for pull requests
citations.supports: Module 9 and 10: opening the diagram pull request

citations.title: Events that trigger workflows - schedule

citations.key_fact: on: schedule uses five-field POSIX cron in UTC by default (an IANA timezone can be set); runs use the latest commit on the default branch; the shortest interval is every 5 minutes; runs can be delayed or dropped at high load, especially at the start of every hour; in public repositories scheduled workflows are disabled after 60 days without activity; @daily-style shortcuts are not supported.

citations.title: GITHUB_TOKEN - GitHub Docs
citations.supports: Module 10: what happens when the drift job opens a pull request

citations.title: BIG-IP Virtual Edition free trial

citations.title: NetScaler VPX FAQ (13.1)

citations.key_fact: VPX Express is free, needs no license file and has no expiry in the newer version (older Express licenses expire one year after download); it has the Standard Edition feature set except Gateway from 12.0-56.20; a retail license is needed to file support cases.
